title: The Propagating Nature of Single- and Multimagnons in LaCrO$_3$
authors: Masoud Lazemi, Fabian J. Mohammad, Ellen M. Kiens, Yorick A. Birkhölzer, Paras Mehta, Emma van der Minne, Stefano Agrestini, Frank M. F. de Groot, Hebatalla Elnaggar
abstract: The dispersion of an excitation is commonly used to infer its microscopic character: dispersive modes are associated with propagation, whereas nondispersive features are often interpreted as localized. This distinction becomes less straightforward for composite excitations, whose spectral maxima can remain nearly dispersionless even when they are built from propagating quasiparticles. Here we use momentum- and temperature-dependent resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) to reveal the origin of multimagnon excitations in antiferromagnetic LaCrO$_3$. Whereas the single magnon disperses strongly, the two- and three-magnon features remain nearly flat. On approaching the Neel temperature, thermal population of the magnon band produces an anti-Stokes branch and opens an additional three-magnon channel involving the creation of two magnons and annihilation of one. Its energy and momentum dependence are reproduced by a thermally weighted multimagnon joint density of states calculations. These results establish thermal population as a means of exposing the propagating constituents hidden within nondispersive composite excitations, and position RIXS as a probe of multimagnon dynamics and, ultimately, magnon-magnon interactions.
summary: This work uses RIXS spectroscopy on LaCrO3 to investigate the nature of magnetic excitations, particularly multimagnons. By measuring spectra across varying temperatures, the authors show that thermal effects reveal propagating magnon components hidden within seemingly localized, multi-magnon spectral features. This establishes temperature-dependent RIXS as a key tool for studying complex magnetic interactions in correlated materials.
main_problem: The study aims to distinguish the true microscopic nature of composite excitations, such as multimagnons, from their observed spectral dispersion, especially when the composite feature appears nearly nondispersive.
main_result: The research demonstrates that thermal population of the magnon band, observed via temperature-dependent RIXS, can reveal propagating constituents hidden within seemingly nondispersive multi-magnon features.
method: The study combines experimental measurements using momentum- and temperature-dependent Resonant Inelastic X-ray Scattering (RIXS) with theoretical calculations like linear spin-wave theory and multimagnon joint density of states calculations.
model_or_system: The physical system is the antiferromagnetic perovskite material LaCrO3. The theoretical framework involves modeling the magnetic excitations using Heisenberg Hamiltonians and calculating joint density of states for single-, two-, and three-magnon processes.
key_observables: Single-magnon dispersion, two- and three-magnon spectral features, anti-Stokes scattering, and temperature-dependent spectral weight changes.
important_parameters: Temperature (especially approaching the Néel temperature, T_N), momentum transfer (Q), and the exchange coupling constant (J1).
main_assumptions: The initial distinction between dispersive (propagating) and nondispersive (localized) modes is complicated for composite excitations; the analysis relies on the Bose-Einstein distribution for magnon occupation.
figures_summary: Figures show RIXS spectra at different temperatures, illustrating the single-magnon dispersion at low T and the emergence of anti-Stokes and new three-magnon channels at high T, compared against spin-wave calculations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the ambiguity of interpreting spectral dispersion for composite excitations, presents RIXS data showing single vs. multi-magnon features at varying temperatures, and concludes by using thermal population effects to confirm the propagating nature of the constituent magnons via theoretical modeling.
why_interesting: The use of RIXS to probe multi-magnon dynamics and magnon-magnon interactions provides a powerful experimental handle on strongly correlated magnetic systems, linking spectroscopic measurements directly to many-body quantum dynamics.
